summary: Describes how http URIs can be fetched using TLS and HTTP/2 to blunt pervasive monitoring. It is not a replacement for https and is vulnerable to active attacks. This RFC is historic.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 8164 lets a server offer its ordinary web pages over an encrypted connection while the addresses stay as plain http. The client checks two things first: that the server's certificate is valid for the site, and that the server lists the site in a standard file. With those checks done, the connection is encrypted but not fully authenticated.

questions: what is opportunistic security for http
does opportunistic http/2 prevent man-in-the-middle attacks
what is opportunistic security for http/2
subtitle: A way to serve ordinary http addresses over an encrypted connection, without the client having to trust the server's identity.

tldr.problem: Encrypting a web connection normally means changing its address from http to https, which is a bigger change than many sites want to make.
tldr.mechanism: The server advertises an alternative service over TLS, and the client checks that the certificate is valid for the origin and that a well-known resource names the origin, before sending http requests over the encrypted connection.
tldr.outcome: The traffic is hidden from someone watching the network, but an attacker in the middle can still interfere, so the RFC calls it opportunistic and says plainly that it is not a replacement for https. It is Historic today.

today: RFC 8164 is Historic, so it is no longer a current standards document, and the unit metadata lists no replacement RFC for it. It was published in May 2017 as an Experimental protocol for serving http URIs over TLS, and it says plainly that this is not a replacement for https and remains vulnerable to active attacks.

sections.title: Goals and Non-Goals
sections.content:
The document describes a use of HTTP Alternative Services to decouple the URI scheme from the use and configuration of the underlying encryption. It lets an http URI be accessed using HTTP/2 and Transport Layer Security with Opportunistic Security.

The usage model is that sites can serve http URIs over TLS. That avoids the problem of serving mixed content while still giving protection against passive attacks. Opportunistic Security does not give the same guarantees as TLS with https URIs, because it is vulnerable to active attacks, and it does not change the security context of the connection. Normally, users will not be able to tell that it is in use: there is no lock icon.

The immediate goal is to make the use of HTTP more robust in the face of pervasive passive monitoring. The secondary, but significant, goal is ease of implementation, deployment and operation: the mechanism is expected to have a minimal impact on performance and to require trivial administrative effort to configure.

Two things are explicitly not goals. Preventing active attacks such as man-in-the-middle attacks is a non-goal. And the specification is not intended to replace or offer an alternative to https, because https both prevents active attacks and invokes a more stringent security model in most clients.
sections.plainLanguage: The aim is to make ordinary web traffic harder to watch on the network, and to do it without asking sites to change their addresses or do much work. What it explicitly will not do is stop someone in the middle of the connection from interfering.

sections.title: Using HTTP URIs over TLS
sections.content:
An origin server that supports the resolution of http URIs can indicate support for this specification by providing an alternative service advertisement for a protocol identifier that uses TLS, such as h2. Such a protocol MUST include an explicit indication of the scheme of the resource, which excludes HTTP/1.1, because HTTP/1.1 clients are forbidden from including the absolute form of a URI in requests to origin servers.

A client that receives such an advertisement MAY make future requests intended for the associated origin to the identified service, provided that the alternative service opts in as described in Section 2.1. A client that places the importance of protection against passive attacks over performance might choose to withhold requests until an encrypted connection is available; if such a connection cannot be successfully established, the client can resume its use of the cleartext connection.

A client can also probe explicitly for an alternative service advertisement by sending a request that carries little or no sensitive information, such as one with the OPTIONS method. A client that already holds alternative services information could make such a request before that information expires, to reduce the delays that might otherwise be incurred.

Client certificates are not meaningful for URLs with the http scheme, so clients creating new TLS connections to alternative services for the purposes of this specification MUST NOT present them. A server that also provides https resources on the same port can request a certificate during the TLS handshake, but it MUST NOT abort the handshake if the client does not provide one.
sections.plainLanguage: The server says, in a header, that the same site can be reached over TLS at a given protocol. The client notes that and may use it for later requests. Client certificates are left out, because a certificate identifies the client and there is nothing here for it to identify.

sections.title: The Server Opt-In and the Well-Known URI
sections.content:
The server might become confused about whether a request's URL has an http or an https scheme, so clients must make additional checks before directing http requests to an alternative service. Clients MUST NOT send http requests over a secured connection unless the chosen alternative service presents a certificate that is valid for the origin. In addition to authenticating the server, the client MUST have obtained a valid http-opportunistic response for an origin using the authenticated connection. The exception is requests for the http-opportunistic well-known URI itself. The RFC gives the exchange: a GET for the well-known path with the scheme recorded as http, answered with a 200 and the media type application/json, whose body is an array of the origins the server will serve over TLS.

The specification describes multiple origins, but only for operational convenience. Only a request made to an origin, over an authenticated connection, can be used to acquire the http-opportunistic resource for that origin, so a request to one form of a name cannot be assumed to cover another form of it.

Clients MUST NOT send http and https requests on the same connection, and MUST NOT send http requests for multiple origins on the same connection.

The http-opportunistic well-known URI is a resource that a client has a valid response for when all of the following hold: the client requested the well-known URI from the origin over an authenticated connection and a 200 response was provided; that response is fresh, possibly through revalidation; it has the media type application/json; its payload, parsed as JSON, has an array as the root; and the array contains a string that matches the origin in question, case-insensitively and character for character, serialised into Unicode as described in RFC 6454. A client MAY treat the resource as invalid if the values in it are not strings.

Allowing clients to cache this resource means that all alternative services need to be able to respond to requests for http resources, and a client is permitted to use an alternative service without acquiring the resource from that service. A client MUST NOT use any cached copy of the resource that was acquired or revalidated over an unauthenticated connection, and a client that uses cached responses MUST ensure its cache is cleared of any response acquired over an unauthenticated connection. Revalidating an unauthenticated response over an authenticated connection does not make the response trustworthy.
sections.plainLanguage: Before sending ordinary http requests over the encrypted connection, the client checks two things: the certificate must be valid for the site being contacted, and the site must have listed that address in a standard file at a standard path. The listing is fetched over the encrypted connection, so a fake server cannot supply it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
On security indicators, user agents MUST NOT provide any special security indicators when an http resource is acquired using TLS. In particular, indicators that might suggest the same level of security as https MUST NOT be used, such as a lock device.

On downgrade attacks, the RFC says one against the negotiation for TLS is possible. Because the Alt-Svc header field likely appears in an unauthenticated and unencrypted channel, it is subject to downgrade by network attackers. In its simplest form, an attacker that wants the connection to remain in the clear need only strip the Alt-Svc header field from responses.

On privacy, cached alternative services can be used to track clients over time, for example with a user-specific hostname. Clearing the cache reduces the ability of servers to track clients, so clients MUST clear cached alternative service information when they clear other origin-based state, such as cookies.

On confusion about the request scheme, HTTP implementations and applications sometimes use ambient signals to decide whether a request is for an https resource, for example by looking for TLS on the stack or for a server port number of 443. This may be because of a limitation in the protocol, since the most common HTTP/1.1 request form does not carry an explicit indication of the URI scheme, or because of how the server and application are implemented. Any security decision based on that information could be misled by the deployment of this specification, because it breaks the assumption that the use of TLS or port 443 means the client is accessing an https URI and operating in the security context that implies. Server implementers and administrators therefore need to examine the use of such signals carefully before deploying this specification.

On server controls, the specification requires a server to send both an alternative service advertisement and host content in a well-known location for http requests over TLS to be sent. Servers SHOULD take suitable measures to ensure that the content of the well-known resource remains under their control. And because the Alt-Svc header field describes policies across an entire origin, servers SHOULD NOT permit user content to set or modify its value.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC is blunt about the limits. The browser must not show a lock icon, because the protection is weaker than https. An attacker on the network can remove the advertisement and leave the connection in the clear. And any server logic that decides whether a request is secure by looking for TLS or port 443 will get the wrong answer once this is deployed.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: The specification registers one well-known URI with IANA. The URI suffix is http-opportunistic. The change controller is the IETF. The specification document is Section 2.3 of RFC 8164.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC asks for one name to be reserved in the registry of well-known URI suffixes: http-opportunistic.

viz.caption: THE EXCHANGE THAT OPTS A SERVER IN

messages.label: GET /.well-known/http-opportunistic
messages.note: Sent over an authenticated TLS connection, with the scheme recorded as http.

messages.label: 200 OK, application/json
messages.note: The body is a JSON array listing the origins the server is willing to serve over TLS.

messages.label: GET / over TLS
messages.note: The client may now send http requests over the encrypted connection, because the certificate was valid for the origin and the well-known resource named it.

viz.caption: THE HTTP/2 EXCHANGE AS THE RFC PRINTS IT

data.title: The http-opportunistic exchange
data.code:
HEADERS
  + END_STREAM
  + END_HEADERS
    :method = GET
    :scheme = http
    :authority = example.com
    :path = /.well-known/http-opportunistic

HEADERS
    :status = 200
    content-type = application/json
DATA
  + END_STREAM
[ "http://www.example.com", "http://example.com" ]

viz.caption: WHAT THE RFC SETS OUT TO DO, AND NOT TO DO

items.title: Resist passive monitoring
items.text: The immediate goal is to make the use of HTTP more robust in the face of pervasive passive monitoring.

items.title: Easy to operate
items.text: Ease of implementation, deployment and operation, with minimal impact on performance and only trivial administrative effort.

items.title: Avoid mixed content
items.text: Serving http URIs over TLS avoids the problem of serving mixed content while still giving protection against passive attacks.

items.title: Not preventing active attacks
items.text: Preventing man-in-the-middle attacks is explicitly a non-goal of this specification.

items.title: Not replacing https
items.text: The specification is not intended to replace or offer an alternative to https URIs.
